newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Onlookers helpless as HK islands activist drowns.
newsitem.headline: Onlookers helpless as HK islands activist drowns.

text.p: Hong Kong activists watched helplessly on Thursday as their leader, protesting Japan's claim to disputed islands, leapt from his ship into the East China Sea, struggled against the raging waters and drowned.
David Chan, leader of 18 activists aboard the protest tanker Kien Hwa 2, began showing signs of distress only moments after he and four others, tied to ropes, plunged into the water.
Chan tried repeatedly to grab his rope and climb back on board, but after about 15 minutes, he stopped moving and his head slumped forward in water stirred up by the vessel's wake.

From the vantage point of this reporter and about 15 others on the fishing boat Hanghai some 50 metres (yards) away, Chan's fellow passengers on the tanker seemed frozen with shock or unaware at exactly what was happening.
It was apparent soon after the five jumped into water that they could not last long. Sensing trouble, three of the swimmers quickly climbed back on deck while Chan and another struggled.
The fourth swimmer was finally able to pull himself up with the help of his rope and people on board, but the protesters did not seem to sense the seriousness of Chan's plight.
By the time the protesters had lifted his lifeless body out of the water, his swimsuit had been ripped open by the strong current while his lifejacket was hanging loose.
One of the protesters began to apply mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, but there was no sign of life.
About 15 minutes later a Japanese rescue helicopter arrived. Officials airlifted the injured swimmer to hospital while others resumed artificial resuscitation on Chan to no avail.
The journalists' fishing boat left the scene with the Japanese officials still attempting to revive Chan.

The death of Chan, a 45-year-old media consultant, was the first in the campaign by ethnic Chinese in Taiwan, Hong Kong and China to force Japan to give up the islands, which Tokyo calls the Senkakus and China calls the Diaoyus.

Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China. Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
The long-simmering dispute flared in July when Japanese rightists built a lighthouse on one of the islands to bolster Japan's sovrignty claim.

Chan's group sailed out of Hong Kong on Sunday, intending to rip down the lighthouse and the Japanese flags there, and plant a red People's Republic of China flag, claiming the islands as Chinese sovereign territory. Taiwan also claims the archipelago.
Stormy seas eventually forced the ship to abandon its landing efforts, and it was due to arrive in the Taiwan port of Keelung early on Friday morning.
